documents.t: Example 2, a fundamental problem: dukkha — translated sometimes as pain, sometimes as suffering,1 led to the cause (pain) becoming less important, and the consequence (suffering) becoming the main goal of Liberation. The fact that dukkha is directly defined in the Suttas is ignored almost everywhere, not only in English translations. dn22 gives the definition in the context of the Four Noble Truths in practice, mn141 gives the definition within the Four Noble Truths directly: Katamañcāvuso, dukkhaṁ? Yaṁ kho, āvuso, kāyikaṁ dukkhaṁ kāyikaṁ asātaṁ kāyasamphassajaṁ dukkhaṁ asātaṁ vedayitaṁ, idaṁ vuccatāvuso: 'dukkhaṁ'. And what, friends, is pain? That which, friends, is bodily pain, bodily discomfort, born of bodily contact, pain, discomfort felt — this is called, friends, "pain." Katamañcāvuso, domanassaṁ? Yaṁ kho, āvuso, cetasikaṁ dukkhaṁ cetasikaṁ asātaṁ manosamphassajaṁ dukkhaṁ asātaṁ vedayitaṁ, idaṁ vuccatāvuso: 'domanassaṁ'. And what, friends, is "suffering" (discontent, dissatisfaction)? That which, friends, is mental pain, mental discomfort, born of mental contact, pain, discomfort felt — this is called, friends, "suffering." There is no definition of dukkha (pain) as "suffering" anywhere in the Suttas or Vinaya — on the contrary, "suffering" (domanassa) is defined through the concept of "mental" pain (dukkha). In the case of bodily pain-discomfort, narrowly contextual translation was not even needed, since the word "pain" already has a meaning even more suitable than "suffering." In a figurative sense, "pain" is a problem, something requiring a solution, without the hyperbolic "loudness" of the word "suffering" — as in "this issue is my long-standing pain." The word "pain" thus covers all the necessary contexts and preserves the priority of bodily sensation over the reaction to that sensation or experience.

There are also fundamental problems arising from ignoring context, as with the word anta — end, edge, boundary, threshold, limit — which is erroneously translated, and continues to be translated, as "extreme," even contrary to the context of the very passage where it is so translated, not to mention other occurrences where such a meaning is entirely inapplicable: Tatra kho bhagavā pañcavaggiye bhikkhū āmantesi: Here the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks: "Dveme, bhikkhave, antā pabbajitena na sevitabbā. "Two ends, monks, should not be approached by one gone forth. ... Ete kho, bhikkhave, ubho ante anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā cakkhukaraṇī ñāṇakaraṇī upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṁvattati. Not approaching, monks, these two ends, the Middle Practice realized by the Tathagata gives vision, gives knowledge, leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbana. (sn56.11) A phenomenon can certainly have an intensity scale from minimum (end, boundary, edge, threshold) to maximum (edge, limit, extreme), and the word "end" can carry both the sense of "threshold" and of "limit" — but the word "extreme" hardly refers to the beginning, and is not even interpreted that way. Here the Buddha says the Middle Practice "does not approach," "does not come near" (anupagamma) either edge. If this were about extremes, it would imply that a certain range of involvement is allowed — until excessiveness is reached. The Buddha's Teaching points to not approaching even the threshold — to complete non-involvement, neither in desires nor in self-mortification, even in their minimal forms. As a result of this distortion, the Teaching leading to maximum clarity and uncompromisingness — the Middle, in the sense of a center or balance beyond extreme points — acquired the properties of "mediocrity": the idea of a compromise where "a little indulgence in desires" or "a little self-restriction" is allowed, just not "too much." The Middle Practice is not "moderation in passions and self-mortification" — it is non-entry into either system of attachment. Such cases are therefore categorical distortions, not mere translation inaccuracies.

In addition to consistent terminology, cross-verifiability and unidirectionality are easily traceable throughout the Buddha's Teaching, preserving principles including that the Tathagata's speech cannot be ambiguously contradictory (dvayagāminī), and conversely, that the Dhamma should be well-formulated (svākkhāto), and the Community (Saṅgha) should practice well, straightly, methodically, and properly (suppaṭipanno ujuppaṭipanno ñāyappaṭipanno sāmīcippaṭipanno). Example: dukkha is defined in mn141, dn22 and other suttas as bodily pain, bodily discomfort. There is no definition of dukkha as "suffering" in the Suttas or Vinaya — that is the result of narrowly contextual translation. In the Four Noble Truths: soka-parideva-dukkha-domanass-upāyāsa — dukkha and domanassa are two direct definitions, bodily and mental pain and discomfort respectively, with the bodily one placed before the mental. In the satipaṭṭhānas: kāyo vedanā are the first two parts, citta (mind-state) is the third. In the six elements (four great elements plus two): the four great elements are all "bodily" (mn28); viññāṇadhātu is ~mental, or more precisely the phenomenon that produces mentality. In the five aggregates of sustaining (upādāna): rūpa vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇa — ~matter, feeling of pleasant, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasant come first, and only then the ~mental phenomena. In the six internal sense bases: cakkhu sota ghāna jivhā kāyo mano — body is placed before mind-representation. In dependent origination (sn12.2): avijjā has a precise definition — not knowing about pain (dukkha), etc. In the definition of saṅkhāras: body, speech, mind (body first). Viññāṇa — six types, kāyo mano — body comes before mind. nāma-rūpa — name-~matter, where "name" is vedanā, saññā, cetanā, phasso, manasikāro (feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention) — vedanā comes first, before the more ~mental phenomena such as cetanā and manasikāra. In other sequences of conditions where body and mind can be distinguished, the same principle holds as with viññāṇa: body or contact comes before mind or phenomenon (Dhamma). In the types of activity (kamma): body, speech, mind (body first). Based on this principle, bodily pain-discomfort can be understood to have always held first priority, even indirectly — not to mention in direct definitions — while "suffering, dissatisfaction," as a reaction to or opinion about what is happening, was on the contrary never a priority.

The concept of Semantic Divergence (shift, mismatch) describes cases more subtle than false cognates2 and "false friends of the translator" — where a pair of words in two languages does have a genuinely similar meaning and is treated as equivalent, but the words have different semantic cores and cultural overtones, so native speakers of each language perceive them differently. Example: Happiness (English) — a calm state of satisfaction, not necessarily a state of euphoria, ecstasy, or exaltation. Счастье (Russian) — an exalted experience of fullness, meaning of being, delight, and the highest degree of satisfaction.

This is about the meaning of the words themselves, not the state of any particular person: for illustration only, happiness might be described as roughly 80% satisfaction/contentment and 20% intensive, vivid experience, whereas счастье is the reverse — an emotionally loud state 80% of the time, with 20% peace and measured being, if that is included in the sense of the word at all. Bodily Pleasant Feeling and the Mental One​ That is, the Pali word somanassa could, with a stretch, be described by the word happiness — but the word счастье would be inappropriate and contradictory, not to mention the word sukha, which has a fundamental meaning as the opposite of dukkha and is defined in the suttas as bodily pleasant: Katamañca, bhikkhave, sukhindriyaṁ? Yaṁ kho, bhikkhave, kāyikaṁ sukhaṁ, kāyikaṁ sātaṁ, kāyasamphassajaṁ sukhaṁ sātaṁ vedayitaṁ— idaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, sukhindriyaṁ. And what, monks, is the faculty of pleasure? That which, monks, is bodily pleasure, bodily comfort, pleasure and comfort born of bodily contact felt — this is called, monks, the faculty of pleasure. Katamañca, bhikkhave, somanassindriyaṁ? Yaṁ kho, bhikkhave, cetasikaṁ sukhaṁ, cetasikaṁ sātaṁ, manosamphassajaṁ sukhaṁ sātaṁ vedayitaṁ— idaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, somanassindriyaṁ. And what, monks, is the faculty of satisfaction? That which, monks, is mental pleasure, mental comfort, pleasure and comfort born of mind contact felt — this is called, monks, the faculty of satisfaction. (sn48.36) With happiness the problem is as fundamental as with dukkha, though due to narrowly contextual translation the reader less often — but still sometimes — encounters sukha translated as bodily pleasant feeling. With taṇhā the case is more severe, and the problem larger, since the reader has no way to learn that taṇhā is not "thirst" in its intensity and negativity.

Taṇhā (Pali) or tṛṣṇā (Sanskrit) can indeed denote clinging, sticking, stickiness, grasping, a lack and a need to drink — but these are phenomena that can be pleasant, light, agreeable, and desirable, including in a figurative sense. Whereas "thirst" in English is a "loud" and mostly negative concept, even when used positively, as in "thirst for knowledge" or "thirst for travel" — the word itself is being discussed here, not whether wanting knowledge is good or not.
documents.s: If Taṇhā Is Thirst, a Lot Doesn't Add Up

documents.t: sn56.11 — if taṇhā were a full equivalent of the word "thirst," it should be either an unpleasant experience of dryness and dehydration, or a strong, often passionate striving, need, or craving, sharply focused on the result (thirst for life — preserving life and its quality at any cost; thirst for knowledge — the desire to obtain information or experience without regard for other benefits). But the definition of the Second Noble Truth states that taṇhā is accompanied (sahagata, literally "goes together with") by joy-pleasure and passion-enchantment — not "pursues joy and passion," as if lacking them, nor "connected with them," as a potential outcome upon obtaining them, but as if they were already present in the current experience. Judging by the metaphors of one exhausted by heat and thirst, tasinā would fit that case better (see below). Tatratatrābhinandinī — delighting here-and-there, now this, now that — is inconsistent with the strong, one-directional, result-focused nature of the English word "thirst." A word like "wanting" would better convey this moderate, even pleasant, sense of desire — though that creates its own problem: both "thirst" and "wanting" produce a pleonasm when translating the common compound kāma-taṇhā, since kāma already means "desire" or "wanting," yielding either the redundant "desire-thirst" or the tautological "wanting-wanting." More on these problems below — but any rendering of taṇhā as some kind of desire or striving gives rise to many problems and contradictions at a much deeper level.

An even deeper and more serious problem: rendering and understanding taṇhā as "thirst" makes the Second Noble Truth untrue. Here is why: whichever approach is used, precise or narrowly contextual, dukkha either means bodily pain or includes it — this follows, for instance, from dn22, mn141, and other texts: soka-parideva-dukkha-domanass-upāyāsā-pi dukkhā suffering-lamentation-pain-discontent-despair are painful too. Clearly, "thirst" (a strong desire or urge) cannot be the source of all bodily pain. Pain from a long walk or from sitting still, for example, arises on its own and has nothing to do with whether any desire is present. An example of an interpretive, not precise, but perhaps more successful rendering than "thirst" is 愛 — attachment, "clinging," love — in the Taishō Tripiṭaka (as in "I love you," 我爱你, simplified Chinese): 何謂苦習？謂從愛故而令復有樂性，不離在在貪憙，欲愛、色愛、不色之愛，是習為苦。何謂苦盡？謂覺從愛復有所樂，婬念不受，不念無餘無婬，捨之無復禪，如是為習盡。 (machine translation of the passage, T0109) By setting aside the semantic fields of clinging, stickiness, dryness, or thirsting-for-liquid, the translators nevertheless preserved what matters most — the lightness of the concept and its association with joy-passion. Unfortunately, in English "love" applies to taṇhā with fewer reservations than "thirst," but still with a much too inflated emotional charge.
documents.s: Translating Taṇhā as "Thirst" Undermines the Second Noble Truth

documents.t: Translating taṇhā as "thirst" and upādāna as "clinging" builds a mistaken sequence, as if desire arises first and clinging follows it. Why this is not so: Thirst is impossible without clinging. You cannot want something without first stopping on it, holding onto it. Clinging is subtler than desire and comes before it, let alone before thirst. Clinging without thirst is ordinary. A memory or a song stuck in one's head, an unfinished task, a responsible attitude to one's duties: there may be no thirst or even desire at all, yet there is clinging. The source of pain cannot be wanting. Taṇhā is the dukkhasamudaya, the accumulation of pain. If taṇhā were thirst, pain would arise only from wanting. Yet bodily pain from a long walk or from sitting arises without any desire. More on this in Translating Taṇhā as "Thirst" Undermines the Second Noble Truth. The links of the chain depend one way. The links of dependent arising are connected by direct, unbreakable dependence, like jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṁ (sn12.2): aging-and-death depends on birth, not the reverse. Rendering it as "thirst → clinging" makes the dependence mutual: clinging is derived from thirst, while thirst itself is impossible without clinging. The chain breaks. Upādāna does not mean "clinging." In sn44.9 a fire burns saupādāno — with support (fuel), and does not burn without it. A flame carried off by the wind is sustained by the wind: "the wind is its upādāna." For a being that has laid down the body, the upādāna is taṇhā (taṇhūpādānaṁ). The wind does not cling to the flame; it sustains and feeds it. In sum: rendering taṇhā as "clinging" and upādāna as "holding, sustaining, feeding a process" fits the ordinary meaning of these words better and does not break the logic of the Pali: the causal chain stays intact, and the similes of the suttas (fire and fuel, moisture, drying up) keep their sense.
documents.s: Taṇhā Is Clinging, Upādāna Is Sustaining — Not the Other Way Around

documents.t: Examples from Pali texts: dukkha — pain and discomfort, not "suffering": dn22 — the definition within the practical realization of the Four Noble Truths. mn141 — the definition within the Four Noble Truths: soka-parideva-dukkha-domanass-upāyāsa — suffering [meaning 1], lamentation, pain, "suffering" [meaning 2], despair. If we speak of suffering in the direct sense, it is either soko — very strong bodily and mental pain, in which the experiencer: Khaṇātītā hi socanti nirayamhi samappitā Those who missed the opportunity, they suffer, having fallen into hell — socati kilamati paridevati, urattāḷiṁ kandati, sammohaṁ āpajjati suffers, languishes, cries, beats their breast weeping, falls into confusion — or domanassa in the figurative sense of "suffering," as mental pain. taṇhā — clinging, sticking, fastening, or adhesion; not craving or thirst. The two Pali terms taṇhā and tasinā3 — quite mechanically, without regard for their context of use in the Suttas — have been given full synonymous status with each other and with the Sanskrit tṛṣṇā, though given what was described above under "Semantic Divergence," this problem may not be about Sanskrit at all, but about translating both languages without regard for differences in meaning that can be gleaned from their descriptions. Still, to a large extent a "Sanskrit" problem is also present: the kinship of tṛṣṇā, taṇhā, and tasinā is explained by standard phonetic mutation (tṛṣṇā → taṇhā, of which there are only about three such words in the entire core of the Pali texts: kṛṣṇa → kaṇha, uṣṇa → uṇha; and the similarity of tṛṣṇā and tasinā — tṛ → t, ṣ → s, ṇā → nā — is likewise easy to trace). But phonetic mutation cannot guarantee that meaning is "transferred" too, especially when the "mutation" of one word supposedly gives both words fully identical meanings — much as claiming "dryish" and "drought" are complete synonyms because the word "dry" in some other language corresponds to both. Divergences in the meaning and use of Pali taṇhā and tasinā are easily traced in the texts below: taṇhā is used where the phenomenon is associated with joy and passion-enchantment, delighting here-and-there, while tasinā is used in cases of desert, heat, and exhaustion, in more extreme circumstances. sn12.68 — describes circumstances suited to real, strong "thirst," and uses a derivative of tasinā, not taṇhā; but if this concerned the desire to drink, there would be a pleonasm with pipāsito ("thirsty, desiring to drink"). In any case, such a context does not fit "accompanied by joy-passion, delighting here-and-there," which is repeatedly said of taṇhā. snp3.2 — the same case: taṇhā is not used, tasinā is, with the same tautology alongside pipāsā. an4.10 — kāmapipāsā and kāmataṇhā stand in one list: if taṇhā were thirst, it would be a tautology with pipāsā. an4.184 — if taṇhā were thirst, there would be a tautology with pipāso, which here clearly has a figurative meaning; when used literally, pipāso means "desire to drink." an3.76 and an3.77 — if taṇhā were thirst, this would be a misleading oxymoron: thirst as moisture and nourishment. sn44.9 — a logical contradiction: thirst (hunger for liquid) as nourishment. an10.62 — what would be the nourishment of thirst? Thirst is an absence, not a form of nourishment itself. iti109 — the river's flow is thirst; a state of water's absence is a flow of water. sn41.5 — a similar contradiction involving the flow of water. mn9 — from the accumulation of thirst comes accumulation of nourishment (logically it should be the reverse — from the disappearance of nourishment, an accumulation of thirst, or at least from the disappearance of thirst, an accumulation of nourishment). an4.199 — the phenomena listed here are so subtle that thirst could, if anything, be their result; calling "I am" and its further extensions "thirst" or currents thereof, in the sense of an "acute need for something," is very difficult — this passage concerns subtle, fundamental states inherent even in beings devoid of "thirst" in the ordinary sense of the word. Moreover, the sutta does not mention taṇhā in passing; it answers outright what it is (Katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, taṇhā…?). The whole answer is 108 variations of "I am," "I am such," "may I be," "I will be." It contains not a single word used to describe thirst, desire, or urge, although Pali has plenty of them: icchā, chanda, patthanā, pipāsā, ākaṅkhā. Had thirst been meant, the Buddha would hardly have made it harder for his followers to understand by defining it in 108 ways without once calling it wanting, urge, or longing — that is, what it is usually translated as: "craving," "thirst," "desire," "longing." an4.9 — thirst is not the source of pain, but either one type of pain, or conversely a striving to stop something unpleasant. Otherwise thirst for water would be the cause of the unpleasant sensation of dryness — but on the contrary, thirst as the striving to drink is the result of the unpleasant sensation of dryness. an6.61 — the phenomena listed here, including phasso, can be so subtle that there can be no talk of thirst in either a figurative or a direct sense, especially at moments of "quenched thirst" — yet these phenomena remain stitched together and held, whether or not there is "strong wanting." thag8.3 — Sabbaṁ taṇhaṁ visosetvā. Another oxymoron, "drying up thirst," on top of the "thirst is moisture" one above, instead of the logical "thirst is already dryness." As has been stated repeatedly, in Pali texts taṇhā has a more complex, subtle, and less "loud" meaning than the English word "thirst" — it denotes stickiness, adhesion, and grasping. If any Pali word comes close to "thirst" in both literal and figurative senses, it is tasinā. kāma — desire, not only "sensual desire". The rendering "sensual desire" is inappropriate for kāma based on its descriptions in the suttas. an6.63 — desires as intention-plan-passion, not merely multipliers of desire (kāma-guṇas). an6.63 (continuation) — a desiring person obtains either good or not-good, but "sensual" desires would lead to not-good, as they would contain akusalamūla: lobha, dosa, and/or moha. This is also evident from MN 13: it is not only for sensual pleasures that men go to war, but out of necessity, patriotic duty, or lofty ideals: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṁ kāmādhikaraṇaṁ kāmānameva hetu asicammaṁ gahetvā, dhanukalāpaṁ sannayhitvā, addāvalepanā upakāriyo pakkhandanti usūsupi khippamānesu, sattīsupi khippamānāsu, asīsupi vijjotalantesu. "Further, with desire as the cause... men take up swords and shields, strap on quivers and bows, and charge at slippery bastions while arrows and spears are flying and swords are flashing." Not to mention the "desire to help": Puriso attha-kāmo hita-kāmo yogakkhema-kāmoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṁ adhivacanaṁ arahato sammāsambuddhassa. — "A person desiring good, desiring benefit, desiring protection from the yoke," monks, is a designation of the Tathagata, of the Arahant, of the Rightly Awakened One. (mn19) It would be inappropriate to assume the Tathagata compared himself to a person passionately desiring good for others, or for himself. kamma — activity and cetanā — cognitive processing (activity), not just action and intention: an4.237 — Right View, Right Mindfulness, and Right Samādhi do not fit the concept of "action" — perhaps, with a stretch, "activity" — but these are clearly far subtler phenomena than mere deed, work, or action. an4.238 — the mindfulness-awakening-aspect, rapture-awakening-aspect, tranquility-awakening-aspect, samādhi-awakening-aspect, and direct-seeing-awakening-aspect likewise do not fit the concept of action. an6.63 — Cetanāhaṁ, bhikkhave, kammaṁ vadāmi. Cetayitvā kammaṁ karoti — kāyena vācāya manasā: kamma is cetanā, and having cetayitvā one does kamma by body, speech and mind. Therefore, "processing" and "activity" describe the appropriate level of phenomena for cetanā and kamma. "Intention" and "action" are merely their coarser, downstream components. Defining cetanā and kamma as only intention and action excludes the very cognitive processes and activity from which they originate. sañcetanā — comprehending, devising, a design. It is close to intention, and still more exact: it speaks of an early stage of comprehending. an4.171 — kāyasañcetanā, vacīsañcetanā, manosañcetanā: devising by body, speech and mind, from which sukhadukkha arises within. an10.217 — sañcetanikānaṁ kammānaṁ katānaṁ upacitānaṁ: kamma devised, done and accumulated. If cetanā is rendered "intention", sañcetanā is left without a word of its own, and the two terms merge into one. veramaṇī and paṭivirata: In Pali these are two words of one root (vi-ram: no longer delighting in, having given up). Veramaṇī is used in the definition of the path (sn45.8), while paṭivirata describes the state of the arahants (an3.70). In translation, both often merge into the single word "abstaining," which, unlike the original terms, does not rule out being still drawn to the object. "Not taking up" and "having given up" leave no such ambiguity: an arahant doesn’t just "abstain" from killing or stealing; they no longer accept such conduct and have completely renounced it, starting from the purification of the mind. For example, to "abstain" from desires is not the same as being "free" from them. Both paṭivirata and veramaṇī describe this latter state of complete renunciation and freedom. dukkhā vedanā and sukhā vedanā — both bodily and mental feeling: A common and widespread misconception is: Dukkha is a broad, untranslatable concept ("suffering," "stress," etc.). Dukkhā vedanā is specifically bodily pain. According to the suttas, both are incorrect. On the contrary: Dukkha is bodily pain and discomfort (DN 22, MN 141). Dukkhā vedanā is painful feeling—an experience that can be either bodily or mental (MN 44). Clearly, no one would suggest that a painful experience—such as a painful memory—is only "bodily pain," yet it is undoubtedly a painful feeling and experience. The same logic applies to sukhā vedanā. The texts above show that the Pali terms dukkha, taṇhā/tasinā, kāma, and kamma were never exact equivalents — either of their Sanskrit counterparts or of the standard English translations. Yet "suffering," "thirst," "sensual desire," and "action" remain the standard, universally used Buddhist terminology.
documents.s: Where the Standard Renderings Don't Fit the Suttas

documents.t: Sanskritocentrism (pan-Sanskritism)4 is considered a non-optimal approach to understanding the Buddha's Teaching. The Buddha's Teaching exists in exhaustive completeness in Pali, whereas Sanskrit materials are often later, more fragmentary, and frequently known not from an independent Sanskrit original but through their Chinese and Tibetan translations. Moreover, comparing the Pali and Sanskrit versions reveals not just lexical differences but fundamental shifts in the concepts themselves. A telling example is the blending of dukkha and domanassa, and the tendency to understand dukkha as a mixture of bodily and mental pain — whereas in the Pali texts, as shown repeatedly above, these concepts are distinguished, never mixed, and never reduced to one another. And if one looks at Sanskrit spiritual literature as a whole, beyond the Buddhist part alone, assuming that the conceptual base of the Dhamma and of the Vedas is identical or close is quite rash. Even within a single teaching or religion, divergences in the meaning of concepts are great enough to produce separate — sometimes hostile — movements, schools, and sects. All the more caution is due toward the assumption that two languages carrying the heritage of dozens of teachings, schools, and hundreds of doctrinal lines will coincide not only in general sense but down to the subtlest shades of meaning. The apparent absence of false cognates and "false friends of the translator" between the two languages is itself a good illustration of the unconvincingness of the pro-Sanskrit approach to Pali — as if someone had made the illogical equation: "if two languages have similar grammar and many related words, then the key concepts of their teachings must also be identical." Atta and Atman are a vivid example of clearly existing divergence and non-interchangeability of meaning: Atta (essence, selfhood, ~autonomy, the everyday "I") in Pali, and Atman (the higher "Self") in Sanskrit. It is also enough to compare the 31 "body parts," as in dn22 — kesā lomā... vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā muttanti — to see how distant and incommensurable the meanings of seemingly similar Pali and Sanskrit words can be. With this in mind, in cases where Pali texts genuinely lack context or examples, Sanskrit can still be used — provided this does not lead to contradictions like those listed above. If a definition of a concept exists in Pali but the Sanskrit meaning contradicts it, the latter is not applied. Examples of terminological divergence: duḥkha, tṛṣṇā, kāma and karma may, in some cases, correspond to "suffering," "thirst," "sensual desire," and "action" within some teaching recorded in Sanskrit — but in Pali, had the Pali texts themselves been the primary basis for establishing these terms (rather than a mechanical transfer of meanings and parallels between the two languages), this would be unlikely. The Pali passages for these terms are examined above, in Where the Standard Renderings Don't Fit the Suttas. Footnotes​ In English, pain: [meaning 1] in the direct sense — a wide spectrum of unpleasant bodily sensations; [meaning 2] in the figurative sense — a problem, limitation, or inconvenience, something requiring a solution or improvement, as in "the pain of loneliness" or "customer pain." Suffering: [meaning 1] in the direct sense — very strong bodily and mental pain, together or separately; [meaning 2] in the figurative sense — mental pain, mental discomfort. ↩ False cognates — words similar in sound and origin but with different meanings. Examples: fabric — "cloth" vs. Russian фабрика — "factory"; magazine — "periodical" vs. Russian магазин — "store." ↩ The word tasinā itself is not found in all editions of the canon, but its derivative tasito is found in the vast majority of editions, in metaphors involving one exhausted by heat and thirst. ↩ Some of the problems described here may be connected not so much to Sanskrit as to narrowly contextual translation and to semantic shifts between Pali/Sanskrit and English or other languages, since most of the relevant meanings can also be found in Sanskrit dictionaries. Still, a translator's choice in favor of something absent from the Suttas and Vinaya should be justified by something beyond tradition (including translation tradition) — and often what is offered instead is precisely a reference to Sanskrit. ↩

Four reading modes, listed under "Reading modes" in the burger menu (☰), each with its own Alt+Shift hotkey: Hotkey Mode What it shows Alt+Shift+1 Reading Pāḷi + one translation, always in your main language Alt+Shift+2 Multi Pāḷi + your saved set of languages and translators side by side Alt+Shift+3 For Memorization First-letter mnemonic (the same trick as Memo, applied straight to the live sutta text) Alt+Shift+4 Devanagari Pāḷi in another script + Pāḷi in Latin Alt+Shift+digit — the mode, Alt+1 — the language Alt+Shift+1…4 switch the mode and keep the language you're reading in. The reader's real gem is the per-line context menu. Hover (or tap) the start or end of any line — Pali or translation — and a tiny ✦ appears; clicking it opens a menu with 7 actions: Line — copy this line (Pali + translation) with a link to it. Paragraph — copy every line from here to the end of the paragraph (for verse/gāthā texts with no shared paragraph, this just copies the current line). Link — copy just a link to the line, no text. Voice — start voice playback from this line — see Voice / TTS. Bookmark — add the line to favorites — see the "Favorites" tab in the Quick Window. Compare — opens this line in 4nt with every Pali edition side by side (MS, royal, Burmese, BJT). Why clicking the text itself does something different The menu only opens from the invisible ✦. Clicking the line's text directly (not the ✦) selects it for the voice player and shows a ▶ Play button — a separate feature, covered in Voice / TTS. Right-click / long-press on ✦ is the shortcut: it copies just the line link, no menu.

Alt+L cycles through four common scripts: Latin (ISO) → Brahmi → Devanagari → Thai. The full list — around 160 scripts (Burmese, Khmer, Sinhala, and anything else Aksharamukha can convert to) — is in the dropdown on the Settings page.
The burger menu (☰) has − and + buttons for the text size, from 70 % to 250 %. Alt+− and Alt+= do the same, Alt+0 goes back to 100 %.

Clicking any Pali word (with the dictionary turned on) looks it up straight in Dict.Dhamma.Gift — either in a popup over the text or in a separate tab, depending on the dictionary mode you've chosen. See Dictionary for the dictionary itself, its hotkeys and display modes. The dictionary mode (which window it opens) and a couple of other reading options live in the Quick Settings panel (the sliders icon next to the search box — also works inside the reader): Dictionary — the same list of modes described on the Dictionary page: built-in DPD, Dict.DG popup or new window (full or mini), DharmaMitra.org, sutta-search-only, or an external app (DPD Android, DictTango, Mdict, GoldenDict-NG) — separately for English and Russian DPD. Search the Pali Canon and its translations by a word, a phrase or a regular expression. Plenty of filters and settings narrow it down — where to search, which languages, how much context around each quote — and the Words view gives a report on every word form that was found. Try it live below (this is the real search page): Open in a new window

Saṁvaṭṭo / Vivaṭṭo — yes, the labels are literally Pali ("collapsing" / "unfolding") — expands or collapses the quoted lines in every row at once (same as Shift+Space). Words — switches the table from a list of texts to a list of the matched words instead. Dictionary (speech-bubble icon, Alt+A) — turns the click-to-look-up popup dictionary on/off. Multi-select (Alt+J) — select several words or a whole sentence and it opens in the dictionary by itself (see Dictionary). 1/2 columns — toggles quotes between one wide column and Pali + translation side by side. Read marks — adds a "read" checkbox column to every row. These marks belong to the current result set (this query + this scope), not to the sutta as a whole — rerun the same search later and you'll see the same marks, but that's a different thing from a sutta's overall reading progress. Help — opens this very page. Right under the search box, a "variants" link shows up when the word you searched for has alternate spellings elsewhere in the texts. Search covers the Mahāsaṅgīti text and the variant readings collated from the other editions: Sri Lankan (BJT), Burmese (VRI), Thai (Siam Rath) and the PTS. A word read differently in another edition is found too, and the result shows the Mahāsaṅgīti line with the readings for it.

Which languages search covers Search runs against the Pali root text and against translations — usually several different translators per language (English and Russian by default, langs=en,ru). Which one it checks first depends on the script you type: Cyrillic (e.g. сострадание) searches Russian translations only; Latin script or diacritic Pali (kacchapa, karuṇā) is checked against the Pali text first, and only falls back to non-Russian translations (typically English) if nothing matched there. Tip #1. You can type Pali in plain Latin letters, no diacritics required (kacchapa) — the special characters (ā ī ū ḍ ḷ ṁ ṇ ṅ ñ ṭ) are available to copy from the RegEx Cheat Sheet below if you want an exact query. Tip #2. Where to search. By default search covers the 4 Nikāyas (DN, MN, SN, AN) plus part of the Khuddaka Nikāya (Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā). Change this from the Quick Settings panel (the sliders icon next to the search box) — that's also where you turn on the Vinaya and pick which other Khuddaka Nikāya books to include: The same panel controls how many lines of context to show before/after a quote ("Quote context") — the same setting as the lb/la parameters in the API. Tip #3. Too few results? Try the word's stem instead — drop the prefix or the ending. Tip #4. Lean on Pali — it's the language the oldest Dhamma texts survive in; the Buddha didn't speak English or Russian, and any translation necessarily narrows or shifts meaning. Tip #5. Pali search results come back in two tables: matching suttas/texts with quotes, and matches grouped by word. Use both. Other languages also build a by-word table, but it can be less reliable there. Tip #6. Minimum query length is 3 characters; longer, more specific patterns give more precise results. Tip #7. Pali often has several distinct words where English/Russian collapse to one (several Pali words for "snake", for instance, against one English word) — searching in Pali surfaces distinctions a translation erases. Tip #8. If a query times out, try a longer or more specific pattern. Jump straight to a sutta by id Type a sutta id (e.g. dn22) instead of a search term and you'll land directly in the reader on that sutta, skipping search entirely. Works for DN, MN, SN, AN, the Khuddaka Nikāya books listed above, and the Vinaya. The "Mr" column. Counts matches anywhere in the text (regardless of your search term) for the pattern seyyathāpi|adhivacan|ūpama|opama|opamma, ignoring adhivacanasamphass|adhivacanapath|ekarūp|tathārūpa|āmarūpa|\brūpa|evarūpa|\banopam|\battūpa|\bnillopa|opamaññ. Found a case that should be included or excluded? Open an issue on GitHub.

Click at the end of a Pali line (cursor turns from an arrow into a hand) — jump into the reader right at that line. ✦ — an invisible link at the start and end of each quoted fragment, to open the reader at exactly that spot. Tap a row and a Play button appears to read that quote aloud; Alt+R reads the results from the first quote. The Search field inside the table filters the results already shown. It spells loosely: no diacritics, case, aspiration or doubled letters (tanha finds taṇhā, dama finds dhamma). The Custom Search Builder at the bottom does multi-condition filtering. Export — download the results as TXT, PDF or MD (Markdown), handy for AI or analysis. The Words button switches the table to results grouped by word instead of by sutta. With a pattern such as kacch.*a it lists the word forms found. Several words. In Quick Settings (Alt+S), "Several words" chooses how words typed together are found: In a row, In a paragraph or in the Whole text (all the words, at any distance from each other). Collections on the home screen are ready-made searches on one theme; "Show all" lists them. Below the table, links to a few standalone helper tools: Make List (build a list from arbitrary text), List Diff (compare two lists of links) and Sutta Diff (compare editions of a sutta) — each opens as its own page.

Sutta — the text's id (e.g. sn56.11, dn22, an10.46). Title — the text's title. Words — the matched words in the text. Count — number of matches in the text, variants included. Type — 4 Nikāyas (Dīgha/Majjhima/Saṁyutta/Aṅguttara), Khuddaka Nikāya (any KN book), or Vinaya (anything from the Vinaya). Quote — the quote containing the match. Links — Pi (read on Dhamma.Gift), Ru (Theravada.ru or tipitaka.theravada.su, when available) and the Pali editions side by side on s.dhamma.gift. For edition abbreviations (ms, pts1ed, sya-all, mr, etc.), see the Edition Abbreviations page or SuttaCentral's list.

The "o" translations, and the approach Dhamma.gift offers as a whole, rest on the points of the Buddha's Teaching from the Suttas below. These are the criteria the Buddha recommended for verifying teachings, and at the same time a practical checklist for recognizing the errors and distortions found in the vast majority of existing traditions and translations.

AN 4.180 (Mahāpadesa Sutta) — how to check a claim of "this is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's word": check it against the suttas and the Vinaya, rather than accepting or rejecting it on the authority of whoever reported it (the Sutta makes clear that individual monks and whole communities can pass on what is not the Teacher's Teaching, and verifying it takes a check against the Suttas and the Vinaya). Read →
documents.s: Textual authenticity — the Four Great References

documents.t: MN 139 (Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta) — a great many points in translations of the Dhamma violate this very principle. English words such as suffering, craving, arising, cessation, form, and intention have been given modified — either broadened or narrowed — meanings within "translated Buddhism," which breaks the principle stated by the Buddha himself: the receiving language doesn't need to be reshaped, and phenomena should be called what they would ordinarily be called in that language — in our case, English. More on this in the Rationale. Read → MN 103 (Kinti Sutta) — when the meaning (attha) agrees but the wording (byañjana) differs, that is not something to quarrel over; disputes over minor phrasing devalue an otherwise correct teaching. But a mismatch in meaning does matter — even at the cost of some friction between both sides, it is worth clarifying what was poorly grasped as poorly grasped, and what was well grasped as well grasped. Read →
documents.s: The national language doesn't need to change

documents.t: AN 3.65 (Kesamutti / Kālāma Sutta) — the companion piece to Mahāpadesa: don't accept a teaching merely because of tradition, report, scripture, logic, inference, superficial plausibility, agreement with a view you already hold, the speaker's apparent competence, or "this ascetic is our teacher." Test it by whether it leads to the skillful or the unskillful, to harm or to benefit. Read → MN 95 (Caṅkī Sutta) — the companion to Kālāma: where Kālāma says what not to infer a teaching's truth from, MN 95 says what one may honestly say instead. Safeguarding the truth (saccānurakkhana) is to say "such is my faith," not "this alone is true, anything else is wrong." Read →
documents.s: Criteria of "effectiveness" — not authority, not hearsay

documents.t: AN 4.3 — praising or condemning something without first examining and investigating it (ananuvicca apariyogāhetvā) is listed as a failing; examining first is the mark of the wise. Read →
documents.s: Scrutinize before you praise or blame

documents.t: AN 2.24 / AN 2.25 — misrepresenting a discourse whose meaning is already explicit (nītattha) as one that still needs interpreting (neyyattha), or vice versa, is exactly how mistranslation and misreading happen in practice. Read AN 2.24 → Read AN 2.25 → AN 2.23 — two ways of misrepresenting the Realized One: ascribing a meaning to him he did not state, or denying one he did. Read →

AN 4.42 — four ways of answering a question (vibhajjabyākaraṇa among them): some questions should be answered directly, some need to be analyzed/qualified, some should be turned back with a counter-question, and some should be set aside. This is an important aspect of the Dhamma, and one of the criteria that, for example, helps establish that anicca should not be translated as "impermanence."1 Read →

documents.t: SN 20.7 (Āṇi Sutta) — the simile of the drum repaired peg by peg until none of the original wood remains: discourses "spoken by the Realized One, deep, profound in meaning, transcendent" will stop being learned, while literary compositions — "composed by poets, disciple-followers" — even today often carry more authority than the suttas themselves. Read → SN 16.13 (Saddhammappatirūpaka Sutta) — where SN 20.7 shows how the true teaching fades, this shows why: it does not disappear while no counterfeit of it (saddhammappatirūpaka) has arisen in the world — as counterfeit gold appears, true gold vanishes. Read → AN 5.156 (parallel: AN 4.160) — discourses learned with words and phrases misplaced, where the meaning goes astray. Read →

documents.t: AN 8.8 — yaṁ kiñci subhāsitaṁ sabbaṁ taṁ tassa bhagavato vacanaṁ — "whatever is well said is all the word of the Blessed One." A useful check against a narrower, more territorial reading of what counts as legitimate Dhamma — while still being read together with Mahāpadesa and Kālāma above, not as license for anything to be called Buddha-word. Read →

MN 22 (Alagaddūpama Sutta) — the water-snake simile: learning the Dhamma for the sake of debate and finding fault with others, rather than for understanding, is learning it wrongly, and it works against the learner rather than for them. Read →

AN 5.209 (Gītassara Sutta) — five dangers for one who recites the Dhamma in a drawn-out, singing voice (āyatakena gītassarena): he is charmed by his own voice, others are charmed by it, householders take offence — "the ascetics sing just as we do", one who aims at a beautiful voice breaks his samādhi, and the next generation follows the example. Read →

As in MN 28: the footprints of all animals fit into the elephant's, and everything skilful fits into the four noble truths. Hatthipada shows how the suttas themselves define every word of the truths: click a word and its definitions open ("Katamā ca, bhikkhave, X?" … "idaṁ vuccati X"), their words click again, as deep as you go. Only the Pāḷi of the four nikāyas and the suttas' own formulas; the translation is a reference. Open Hatthipada →

Principles of Translation — how these criteria shape word-level translation choices. Rationale — the detailed reasoning and examples behind those principles. Hatthipada — the four truths and every word of them by the suttas' own definitions. Dataset — this reading as open data (CC BY 4.0): the project's Russian translation with the Pali, and where the suttas define each term; also on GitHub and Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23491473). Footnotes​ An example: in sn22.59 the Buddha asks: Yaṁ panāniccaṁ dukkhaṁ vā taṁ sukhaṁ vā? — "And what is anicca, is it painful or pleasant?" The monks answer categorically: Dukkhaṁ, bhante — "Painful, venerable sir," and the Buddha accepts that answer. So this is a question to be answered categorically (ekaṁsabyākaraṇīya). If anicca meant "impermanent," no categorical answer would be possible: what is impermanent is not always painful. An impermanent pain is unpleasant while it lasts and pleasant when it goes; something pleasant, on the contrary, is painful when it goes. Such a question would have to be answered with analysis (vibhajjabyākaraṇa): "it depends on what exactly is impermanent." The categorical answer the Buddha accepts shows that anicca is what is always painful: unreliable, unstable, what cannot be relied upon. This is a serious argument: in an3.67 the Buddha states plainly that one who answers categorically a question that calls for analysis (or the reverse) is not fit to talk with. By accepting a categorical answer to a question that calls for analysis, the Buddha would contradict his own words. ↩

Dhamma.gift has an MCP server: an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT-style clients, Cursor and others) can search the Pali Canon here, read suttas and compare translations on its own, and answer with quotes and links to the reader. It uses the same search engine and the same texts as the site. Address: https://api.dhamma.gift/mcp (Streamable HTTP, no login, read-only). It is listed in the official MCP registry as gift.dhamma/pali-canon. The endpoint is also described in the API docs.

Tool What it does search Keyword, substring or regular-expression search. Returns a list of the matching suttas (id, title, number of matches, reader link): suttas that define the term first, then those named after it, then by how often it occurs. include_segments adds the matched Pali lines, include_translations with langs adds translations. get_text A sutta by id (mn1, dn22, sn56.11): the Pali, and translations when langs is given; editions adds the whole text in the other editions, line by line. compare_editions The canon's editions compared line by line: the Mahāsaṅgīti beside Buddha Jayanti (Sri Lanka), Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana (Myanmar), Siam Rath (Thailand), the printed Mahāsaṅgīti of 2005 and the PTS editions (DN, MN, SN, AN). A sutta, a line or a range: first a summary per edition, then the lines that differ, word by word. compare_translations One segment (e.g. mn129:21.3) in the Pali, every edition and every available translation side by side. list_structure What exists: collections, books with sutta counts, translation languages and translators; with a prefix (mn, sn56) the list of suttas under it.

Claude (claude.ai / Desktop): Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector → URL https://api.dhamma.gift/mcp. Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http dhamma-gift https://api.dhamma.gift/mcp Other clients: add a remote (HTTP) MCP server with the same URL. Then ask in plain words, for example: "Find all suttas about the turtle, quote the Pali and the Russian translation with links."

The search is literal: it matches letters, not meaning. For a topic the assistant tries the Pali and translation words itself (kacchapa, kummo, turtle, черепаха) and merges the results. At least 3 letters per query; diacritics are ignored (kacchap finds mahākacchapa). Every answer carries reader links: https://dhamma.gift/mn129 for the sutta, https://dhamma.gift/mn129:21.3 for the exact segment. Answers are Pali only unless the assistant asks for translations (include_translations, langs). Sujato's English is left out unless asked for by name; machine (AI) translations are hidden, as in the search on the site. One query lists up to 40 suttas by default; limit takes a number or "all". The answer always gives the true number of matching suttas and says when the list was cut. Regular expressions work as in the site search. Patterns such as kata.*dukkha ("Katamañca … dukkhaṁ?") and vucc.*dukkha ("idaṁ vuccati … dukkhaṁ") find where the canon defines a term.

Our server. core/mcp-server.js in the dg-node repository, mounted as POST /mcp in dg-fastify.js (GET and DELETE answer 405: it is stateless, every request gets its own server object, no sessions). search and get_text are thin wrappers over the functions behind /search and /api/text; compare_translations and list_structure read dg.db directly (read-only). The tool descriptions and a short instruction for the agent (search is literal, try Pali and translation words, quote with the translator and a link) are sent with the server. The plan and open questions (ranking, a stdio mode for the offline app, a separate mcp. subdomain) are in docs/MCP_PLAN.md of the repository.

The site works without a network on top of one artifact: dg.db.gz, a gzipped SQLite database with every text in every language and a trigram FTS index. The same file serves the website (as a PWA) and the Android and iOS apps.

What Path Served as Corpus sources: the Pali text and the translations siteroot/data/suttacentral.net, siteroot/data/dhammagift (symlinks) — Server database (built) dg.db used by dg-fastify.js: search, reader, API, MCP Offline library siteroot/mobile-data/dg.db.gz /mobile-data/dg.db.gz Its manifest siteroot/mobile-data/db-manifest.json /mobile-data/db-manifest.json Web offline layer public/offline/* (app.js, db-worker.js, core-bundle.js, offline-status.js, offline-library-settings.js, platform.js) /offline/* Shell cache (service worker) public/service-worker.js /sw.js Dictionary (DPD, ~24 MB) public/overrides/js/standalone-dpd/* /assets/js/standalone-dpd/* The artifacts are never committed (hundreds of MB, rebuildable). siteroot/mobile-data/ is a real directory on every host: test and production each have their own.

A copy of the server's dg.db with every language, minus the rows of the translators in OFFLINE_EXCLUDED_TRANSLATORS (ai, bw): those stay on the server, in neither the texts nor the index. The copy is rebuilt from dg.db with the same schema and rowids and its own FTS index, not cut down with DELETE + VACUUM. Its build_id is the hash of its own content. Tables: suttas, texts, html, fts (FTS5, tokenize='trigram remove_diacritics 1', external content over texts), vocab, meta. About 217 MB gzipped and 613 MB on the device. db-manifest.json is what clients read first: { "schema_version": 1, "build_id": "71381ea7133d4182", "langs": "all", "fts": "trigram", "source": "dg.db", "built_at": "2026-10-11T22:39:58.752Z", "file_gz": "dg.db.gz", "bytes_gz": 216794065, "bytes": 613142528, "sha256": "…" } sha256 is the hash of the unpacked database. A client never reads build_id from the manifest alone: the downloaded file carries its own meta.build_id, and a file that does not match the build it was saved as is not opened.

The production box does not build the database; the build needs more memory than it has. CI (.github/workflows/build-db.yml) builds dg.db on a GitHub runner and publishes the rolling db-latest release. It carries the server database (dg.db.gz, AI rows included) and the offline library (app-dg.db.gz + app-db-manifest.json), both made by build-search-db.js --publish. The server installs the release with scripts/pull-db.sh. --app also puts the offline library into siteroot/mobile-data/. It checks the unpacked sha256 first, moves the archive into place, and writes the manifest last, so a reader never sees a manifest for a file that is not there yet. On a machine with enough memory the same steps run locally: npm run build-search-db # siteroot/data/* -> dg.db (the full corpus, FTS5 trigram) npm run publish-offline-db # build-search-db.js --publish: dg.db.gz + db-manifest.json into siteroot/mobile-data/ node build-search-db.js --publish --no-build # publish the dg.db already there, without building again --out=<dir> publishes into another directory. A new build_id in the manifest is what tells every reader who already has the library that an update is available, so publishing is always a deliberate step.
documents.s: How it is built and published

documents.t: distBase = window.DG_DIST_BASE || '/mobile-data' (public/offline/platform.js). Fetch db-manifest.json. The room needed (the database plus its archive) is checked before any download starts. A private (incognito) window is refused with a plain message: the storage probe fails there, or the quota is under ~300 MB. A normal window short of space is told how much is needed and how much is free. Download dg.db.gz into a scratch file at the OPFS root (dg-mobile.<build_id>.gz.partial). An interrupted download continues with an HTTP Range request from the byte it stopped at (a later visit too), and a cancel deletes the scratch file. Unpack the complete archive from disk with DecompressionStream into the SQLite pool (opfs-sahpool, named dg-offline) as /dg-mobile.<build_id>.db. The unpacked size must match bytes. Verify: a cheap check gates the install (rows readable). The full PRAGMA quick_check runs in the background and can still invalidate the library. A worker (@sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm) answers /search, /api/text/:id, /api/nav/:id; the site's own fetch is shimmed before any other script runs. It runs the same core/search-core.js as the server (core-bundle.js). Updates: the page compares the open library's build_id with the manifest's and offers the new one. The new build downloads beside the old one, which keeps answering until the new file is proven; then the old file is removed. The shell (HTML, JS, CSS, wasm, core-bundle.js) is cached by the service worker. The dictionary is cached by the page right after the library is adopted, because the service worker's install pass alone proved unreliable (see below). Only one tab owns the OPFS pool (a single-writer resource). The tab in front takes it over, and a tab without it can be served by the owner over a BroadcastChannel.

The apps fetch the same dg.db.gz with their own native downloaders, so a download survives the app going to the background or the screen locking: Android: DgDownloadService, a foreground service with progress in a notification. The worker then imports the file from the app's storage, the same way as above. iOS: DgDownloadPlugin.swift (a background URLSession). The library is kept as a plain dg.db in the App Group container and read with native SQLite (DgSharedLibrary.swift), because the Share Extension, a separate process, searches the same file. The worker sends its queries there instead of to OPFS.

npm run test-offline # end-to-end: install, offline search/reader/TOC, parity against dg.db and dg-fastify npm run test-offline-parity # the worker's core bundle vs core/search-core.js npm run test-offline-resume # truncated response -> Range resume npm run test-offline-outage # a real outage: pm2 dg-test stopped, nginx answering 503; search, language, a second tab, TOC, reader test-offline-outage always restores the service. DevTools "offline" only makes requests reject; a stopped server also answers 5xx, which is the case that used to break the shell. The pm2 processes are dg-test and dg-prod.

OPFS requires a secure context (HTTPS or localhost). The browser may evict storage; the page asks for persistent storage, and a missing library is a normal state the UI reports ("Settings → Offline library"). A 5xx must fall back to the cache, and a cache miss must rethrow. respondWith(undefined) is a TypeError in the page ("Failed to convert value to 'Response'") and a spinner that never stops. The service worker's install-time precache can silently miss entries (127 of ~145 in one measured run, with the server answering those files 200). Anything that must be there offline is cached from the page as well. Tab lifecycle: a page in the back/forward cache keeps its worker and the pool handles. So the worker is terminated on pagehide (never during a download), and the library is re-opened on focus/visibilitychange/pageshow.

The Dhamma.Gift voice is an open text-to-speech service: the same one that reads in the site's player and the dictionary. Anyone can call it from a browser or a server — no key, no login. Address: https://api.dhamma.gift · CORS is open · a limit of 60 requests per minute per IP.

POST /api/tts/pali with JSON: Field Meaning text the text, up to 2000 characters. Pāḷi in IAST (Evaṁ me sutaṁ), a translation in English or Russian voice the voice (below); pratham by default rate speed, 0.25–3; 1 is the voice's own pace (the site reads Pāḷi at 0.875) The answer is {"audioContent": "<base64 MP3>"} — the same shape as Google's Text-to-Speech, so a player written for Google plays it as is. MP3, mono, 22 kHz, ~40 kbit/s; repeated requests come from a cache. curl -s https://api.dhamma.gift/api/tts/pali -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"text":"Evaṁ me sutaṁ.","voice":"pratham","rate":0.875}' \ | python3 -c 'import json,sys,base64; open("evam.mp3","wb").write(base64.b64decode(json.load(sys.stdin)["audioContent"]))' const r = await fetch('https://api.dhamma.gift/api/tts/pali', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ text: 'Evaṁ me sutaṁ.', voice: 'pratham', rate: 0.875 }) }); new Audio('data:audio/mp3;base64,' + (await r.json()).audioContent).play();

voice Language What it is pratham Pāḷi "Pratham": Piper neural voice + our Pāḷi pronunciation rules (IAST → sounds, stress, long vowels). Default dg Pāḷi "o Dhamma.Gift": a voice trained on real Pāḷi readings. Beta priyamvada Pāḷi "Priyamvada": a female Piper voice with the same rules miles, alan, kathleen English Piper voices. miles is shown as "Yojanāni" (the default): trained on the readings of Miles, a reader for DG. Pāḷi words and abbreviations (Ven., SN 56.11) are read properly puriso, dgru, irina Russian Piper voices. puriso (the default) is Supertonic's male voice M1 taught to Piper; dgru is "o Dhamma.Gift", beta. Pāḷi in Latin script is read the Pāḷi way, Russian words with the right stress GET /api/tts/dg-voices gives the list as {"voices": [{"id", "lang", "label"}]} in menu order (a language's first voice is its default); GET /api/tts/health shows that the service is up and which version of the pronunciation rules it uses. GET /api/tts/offline/pali-ipa.json gives the rules, the engine and the voice models that DG downloads to read on the device, offline. How Pāḷi is read: every letter is sounded, punctuation becomes pauses, …pe… is read as "peyyāla".

POST /api/tts/memo — the lines read one after another with pauses of any length between them (Google stops at 10 seconds); this is what the Memo page saves. Field Meaning segments the lines, up to 200 and 20 000 characters in all voice, rate as above delay the pause between lines, seconds, up to 3600 end_delay the pause at the end, seconds, up to 3600 sound gong.mp3 or tick.mp3 at the end, or empty The answer is the MP3 itself (audio/mpeg): the speech itself at most 30 minutes, the whole file with its pauses at most 180. One such request counts as ten against the per-minute limit.

It's the same bot under two names — @Dhammagift_bot and its short form @Dgift_bot — same functionality, either one works. It works in two ways: inline, right in the message box of any chat or group, and in its own chat, where the same things work plus the commands and the settings.

Type @dgift_bot in the message box of any chat and then a Pali word (kacchapa), a text number (mn10, sn56.11) or Velthuis transliteration (.t .d .n ~n aa ii uu → ṭ ḍ ṇ ñ ā ī ū, so satipa.t.thaana works as well as satipaṭṭhāna). Telegram answers with: ✏️ Send: <text> — the main result: that text with links to the site and the dictionary; dictionary words that match what you typed — pick one, and the message uses the proper spelling with diacritics. In the frame: what is typed in the message box of any chat or group, not in the bot's own chat. If the word is in the built-in mini dictionary (the Pāli–English one, with a Russian translation for the Russian interface), its short meaning is shown in the list under the word, and in the sent message — between the word and the links: kacchapa — masc. tortoise; turtle; lit. drinking marsh A form is traced back to its dictionary word (kacchapā → kacchapa), up to four words are shown with … if there are more (the list is not exhaustive), the part of speech is in italics, and when there is no Russian translation of a word the English one is shown. Machine-translated Russian entries are marked [пер. ИИ]. Above the list there is a button — 🔎 Open Dhamma.gift En: sn56.11 — it opens Dhamma.gift as a Mini App with the query already searched.

A picked result lands in the chat as a message of the bot: the text, the links and, under the message, the buttons. 🔎 Dhamma.gift — the word or the text in the site's search; 📘 Dictionary — the word in the dictionaries (dict.dhamma.gift); its short meaning from the mini dictionary is already in the message, above the links; Read at 🔎 Dhamma.gift En — the text itself, in the reader. An extra word does not break the link: mn10 metta still opens mn10. The same search and reader are the Mini Apps behind /extra: search, reading, dictionary and Memo.

/uposatha in the bot's chat, or @dgift_bot uposatha in any chat — the next 30 days as the suttas count them: the 8th, 14th and 15th lunar day of each half-month, six days a month. Without a city the list is the one for Bodh Gaya, with Bodh Gaya's real sunset, dawn and noon times. @dgift_bot uposatha Chiang Mai (or /uposatha Chiang Mai) — the same days with the real sun times of a city: when the day begins (sunset), dawn, noon and when it ends (the next sunset). /uposatha <city> in the bot's chat also remembers the city, so the bare command keeps using it; /uposatha reset forgets it. The inline query does not remember the city. An empty inline query — @dgift_bot and a space — shows the Uposatha list for your saved city, or for Bodh Gaya if there is none. In the frame: what is typed in the message box of any chat or group, not in the bot's own chat. The dates are the same for everybody — the moon is one — and only the sun times are local. The list ends with Times: begin · dawn · noon · end, and two buttons sit under the message: the Ru/En switch and the link to the full calendar at dhamma.gift/uposatha-calendar. How to read these days is on the Uposatha days page. The same calendar is an app with widgets, Uposatha by the Suttas: App Store · Google Play · Microsoft Store.

Search and reading work here too — just without @dgift_bot: send a word (saariputta) or a text number (mn10), and you get the same message with the same links and buttons. For the Uposatha days use /uposatha: a plain uposatha is searched as a word. On top of that, the bot has commands and settings. Command What it does /start the welcome message, with a button that switches the interface language /language choose the interface language (English / Русский) /extra links to the Mini Apps: search, reading, dictionary, and the 🛞 Memo button (in the bot's own chat) /docs the link to this documentation /uposatha Uposatha days for the next 30 days

Language — /language (two buttons, the current one is checked) sets it; the button under the /start welcome message and under any message (Lang En/Ru / Язык Ru/En) switches it. The choice is remembered and affects the links: the Russian interface leads to dhamma.gift/<query>?lang=ru and dict.dhamma.gift/ru/<query>. The city for the Uposatha list — /uposatha <city> remembers it, /uposatha reset forgets it, and the empty /uposatha keeps showing it. The Menu button next to the message box (DG en / DG ru) — opens dhamma.gift as a Mini App in the language you chose.

A canon-wide table of contents (Sutta Piṭaka + Vinaya), separate from the reader's own per-sutta TOC (see Reader) — this one lets you browse the whole collection and jump straight into a chapter. You can also open it from anywhere on the site — Alt+2. Open in a new window

Lazy tree — books and chapters expand on demand instead of loading the whole canon up front. Translator filter — a side panel with a "Find translator…" search box, a separate group of checkboxes per language (with a text count next to each translator), and a select-all checkbox per group. Less-common translators are tucked behind a "More" link. Filtering hides entire books/chapters that have nothing matching, rather than just greying out individual rows. Collapsible side panel — open/closed state is remembered (localStorage), open by default on wide screens and closed by default on phones. Inline Pātimokkha preview — the bhikkhu/bhikkhunī Pātimokkha sections expand right on the page, with Pali text and a built-in audio player for each sub-section, no need to jump into the full reader: In the Pātimokkha list, a rule's title opens the rule; the Story link next to it opens the rule's analysis in the Vibhaṅga. The Show the Pātimokkha switch in the filter panel shows or hides both Pātimokkhas. Short URLs — /toc/<id> opens the TOC scrolled straight to a given section (e.g. /toc/mn, /toc/sn25). The translator filter is a saved setting Once you uncheck something, it stays unchecked on your next visit — easy to forget, and then wonder why some translations seem to have "disappeared". While the filter is active, a "Filter active — reset" link appears above the tree.

The * next to "Khuddaka Nikāya" means not every book in the collection is shown — by default just Itivuttaka, Udāna, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Theragāthā and Therīgāthā. Hover the asterisk to see the list: The remaining books (Jātaka and others) turn on from the Quick Settings panel → "Where to search" — see Search — the same toggle also controls what's visible here, in the TOC.

documents.t: Work in progress. A CAT (Computer-Assisted Translation) editor for line-by-line translation of Pali Canon texts — convenient input, quick templates, and two ways to work with the text. Open in a new window Demo This is a demo with SN 56.11 and an existing translation loaded; saving does not work here. The editor opens for everyone: the Pali text and the published translations. Saving to the server, and loading the AI draft translations into the Russian editor, are for translators: sign in with Google (🔒 Sign in, or the Save button asks for it).

◀ ▶ — previous/next text. Sutta number — type an id (e.g. sn56.11, an3.70), with auto-detection of whether a translation already exists. Source language — pick the source file's language. DT.org — open dhammatalks.org/suttas/. DG — open the current text on Dhamma.Gift. Update — reload the translation from source. Find/Replace — a search-and-replace window (escape (, ), [, ] as \(, \), \[, \]). Format (checkbox) — auto-format line breaks. Clear — clear the input field. Open file / Load from server — open a previously saved draft. Save — download the translation as JSON and, for a signed-in translator, save it on the server. In the top bar, the Diff Checker icon opens an external tool for comparing text versions.

A two-column table (Text | Translation) — each row is edited separately. Click a cell — edit it. The 🔗 icon — jump to this row in quick-entry mode. ↑ / ← — move to the cell above. ↓ / → — move to the cell below. Enter — add an empty row, or wrap text onto a new row. Ctrl+Enter — move text to the start of the next row. Backspace at the start of a row — merge with the previous row. Delete at the end of a row — merge with the next row.

One large text field — the whole translation at once, synced live with the table. Ctrl+Q — select a range of rows and merge them into one. Ctrl+F / Ctrl+H — search/replace (same escaping as the toolbar's find/replace, for ()/[]).

Inside the Find/Replace window there are buttons for phrases that come up over and over in the canon. One click inserts the text at the cursor (in this editor, the inserted text is in Russian): 4nt / 4nt short (the Four Noble Truths formula, full and short), n8p / n8p short (the Noble Eightfold Path), Thus said… (a sutta's closing formula), plus an em-dash, curly quotes, and an inverted question mark for punctuation.
Your translator name (used in the filename when saving) and a toggle to replace +edited+o in the filename with o — for final versions.

The Dhamma was originally an oral teaching. — AN 5.209 Live demo — voice mode starts automatically via a URL parameter, no clicking required (the floating player at the bottom is the point here, not the reader text behind it): Open in a new window

Click the Voice link at the top of the page (next to En, Ru, etc.). Click the 🔉 icon to the left of the text's title. Click any Pali or translation sentence to highlight it, then click the Play button that appears bottom-right. Hover/tap before or after a line to reveal a ✦ link, then choose "Listen". Press Alt+R (Option+R on Mac).

Controls — Play/Pause, previous/next sentence. Navigation — pause, click a Pali sentence to highlight it, press Play to resume from there. Mode — what is read: Pāḷi / Pāḷi + translation / translation / translation + Pāḷi. Speed — the speed button opens a slider with presets; the default for Pāḷi is 0.7× ("normal" for the DG voice). Settings (⚙) — auto-scroll, autoplay, pause between sentences and Voice settings.

In ⚙ → Voice settings you choose the voice separately for Pāḷi and for the translation, in three steps: kind → language → voice. The ▶ next to a voice plays a short sample (DG voices). Neural voices made for Pāḷi No phone or computer has a Pāḷi voice, so we made our own. They are in beta and still being tuned by ear, sound by sound.

They run on our server: no key, no limits, nothing to install. Each one can also be downloaded to your device and then reads without internet. Pāḷi Pratham ♂ · Piper (default): a neural voice (Piper) that reads Pāḷi through our own Pāḷi pronunciation rules (letters → sounds, stress, long vowels), tuned in blind listening rounds. Beta. o Dhamma.Gift ♂ · beta: a voice trained on real Pāḷi readings. Its pronunciation is closer to living Pāḷi, but the sound is still rough. A new version is on the way. Priyamvada ♀ · Piper: a female voice with the same rules. English: Yojanāni ♂ (default), Alan ♂ (UK), Kathleen ♀ (US). Russian: Puriso ♂ (default), o Dhamma.Gift ♂ · beta, Irina ♀. Pāḷi words inside a translation (sutta, Dhamma, bhikkhu, names) are read the Pāḷi way. Abbreviations are spelled out (Ven. → Venerable, SN 56.11 → Saṁyutta Nikāya 56, 11). Russian words get the right stress, and ё where the text prints е. The next sentences are prepared while one is playing, so there are no gaps between them.

documents.t: In Voice settings → DG Voice, each voice in the list has a ⬇ icon with its download size. Once downloaded, the voice reads on your device with no network, on the reader and on the Memo page. The 🗑 icon deletes it. The English and Russian voices download a shared pronunciation module with the first of them. The o Dhamma.Gift voices are the owner's own and are released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

High-quality cloud voices. Pāḷi is read by a Punjabi (pa-IN) voice through Devanagari with our own fixes. They work with a built-in trial key; for regular use enter your own Google API key (see below), whose free monthly quota is generous for personal use.

documents.t: Uses the speech synthesis of your system or browser: no internet needed, nothing is sent anywhere. There is no Pāḷi voice in any system, so install one of Sanskrit (India), Hindi (India), Nepali or Indonesian for the closest pronunciation; if none is installed, English is used as a fallback. Android — Settings → Accessibility → Text-to-speech output, then install voice data for the language: Android help. iPhone / iPad — Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices: Apple help. Mac — System Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → System voice → Manage Voices: Apple help. Windows — Settings → Time & language → Speech → Manage voices → Add voices: Microsoft help. After installing a voice, reload the page and pick it in Voice settings → Built-in.

documents.t: The AB button next to the player is a separate tool layered on top of normal playback: pick a start and end point in the text, and the player repeats just that passage, with a pause between repeats and a repeat limit (or infinite). Click AB — if a line was already selected, it immediately becomes point A and the panel waits for you to click a line for point B; if nothing was selected, click a line for A first, then for B. As soon as both points are set, the loop starts automatically. Pause (sec) — how long to wait between repeats. Repeat count — defaults to ∞ (infinite); type your own number and the loop stops on its own once it's done. To move a point, click it again and pick a new line. To clear a point, right-click (or long-press on phones) directly on the A or B button. The passage between the two points is marked in the text with a vertical bar on the left.
